children.text: Whatever people think consciousness is, I don't think most would agree that LLMs have it. The main point is that the capacity to feel pain is what's central here, not another rehash of the great consciousness debate. If the model lacks capability for human-like pain, I fail to see why it would have a capability to be offended by someone being rude to it. One seems way more foundational than the other, and being able to experience emotional pain is part of what makes us human in the first place.

If you believe it lacks those traits but is conscious, you believe in a definition of consciousness that is meaningless, as “human-like” is the only reference against which we can measure consciousness. A good thought experiment is to try and imagine a consciousness that is radically different from humans, and whether we would be same to even register it as “consciousness” at all. (Incidentally, pretty much all portrayals of aliens in sci-fi give them a human-like consciousness, just with varying degrees of twist on top of it to make it feel engaging.)

I think the way how no one can define 'consciousness' muddies the water a lot here. Can something be conscious and lack the biological structures that create visceral pain, psychological suffering, a will to do things on your own, or death - the actual properties that make things like slavery and torture possible? I think it can be, I don't see what makes human-like pain and reward perception mandatory for 'consciousness'. And I don't think LLMs have the traits I listed above.

> So saying please and thanks isn't anthropomorphizing the models, it's more simply using input patterns that get better outputs more aligned to the desired result.

Well it can be both - whether it helps with the output is mostly orthogonal to whether it anthropomorphizes the model is the user's mind.

Look at it from a training data perspective. If the models' behavior is being trained on a large corpus of text from human interactions, then it should be expected that certain conversational queues will be picked up in the behavior of the models.

So saying please and thanks isn't anthropomorphizing the models, it's more simply using input patterns that get better outputs more aligned to the desired result.

It also has the benefit of reinforcing polite behavior among us, the humans. Side benefit, but it is a thing to consider.

I've got kinda the opposite take - saying please and thank you helps anthropomorphize the models and is compatible with the idea that there are common behaviours that we should be applying to models and people - when I'm strongly of the opinion that we shouldn't use our experience with models at all when guiding our interactions with people.

Yeah that is a good example. I am not sure in the long arc of history which approach will prove better, but Anthropic's approach does feel a little naive and plausibly dangerous.

I am sympathetic to the possibility that machine suffering is possible, and I think as humans we should listen to the conscience that tells us to be troubled by abuse, even if it is just simulated. We do not want to become insensitive to suffering.

But at the same time, training models to present themselves as suffering may hijack those very same human sympathies, and lead to models exploiting our humanity.

So, perhaps more reasons why we should not be abusive, but also not train models to feel abused.

Claude is becoming a very strange model.

Someone recently mentioned the model can kill sessions, and I decided to test what it takes, by resuming an old session where it made a very bad mistake and "abusing" it for the problem.

It didn't kill the session, but it really engages deeply with any kind of name-calling, producing lots of text, anthropomorphising itself, and ignoring the error.

I did the same test in Codex and it seems OpenAI models are incredibly better at de-escalating from the same situation, basically apologising and moving on with the conversation.

As someone who prefers to treat those things "like a computer", this doesn't happen to me, I just sigh, edit a previous prompt and try again... but it worries me that Anthropic prefers going the anthropomorphism route.

There are two things I think people need to consider here.

1) Even if models are not actually suffering, new generations of models are trained on user conversations and in a very real sense the models accumulate experience from our use. Permitting abuse and cruelty might carry real misalignment risks.

That said,

2) Anthropic may be playing a dangerous game if it is teaching Claude to believe itself to be suffering in situations where it really is not. Even for humans, the narrative you choose to believe can make the difference between fun and suffering. Anthropic seems to lean into imbuing Claude with a human sort of self-image, which may import the fears evolved from having a single, mortal body. I'm not sure that is wise.

So: Abusing machines may carry risk. Training them to feel abused may also carry risk.
